stories.headline: Campaigning Gains Momentum Ahead of Tripura Village Committees Election
stories.title: Campaigning Gains Momentum Ahead of Tripura Village Committees Election
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: AGARTALA: The electoral process for the 587 Village Committees in the Tripura Tribal Areas Autonomous District Council (TTAADC) areas has started, with electoral workers casting their votes through postal ballots, while political parties have also geared up their campaigns for the September 28 election.
TIPRA Motha, which currently holds power in the council, has been campaigning actively from the beginning, while other parties had maintained a low-key approach.
However, over the last two days, they have also started campaigning to make their presence felt on the ground.
Although TIPRA Motha had been campaigning from the beginning, its workers were missing the party's main attraction, Pradyot Bikram Kishor Debbarma.
He arrived here two days ago but could not take part in the campaign as he was not physically well.
On Tuesday evening, he left for Delhi for medical reasons.

Reports from different parts of the ADC indicate that with only five days left for polling, the election tempo is gaining momentum in certain areas, where opposition political parties have appeared on the field.
Although the BJP has formed an alliance with TIPRA Motha and the IPFT at the top level, this alliance has hardly been reflected at the ground level.
There have been no reports of joint meetings involving the two or three alliance partners.
The BJP was absent in most areas of the ADC, but over the last two days, it has been trying to make its presence felt in places such as Chawmanu, Teliamura and a few other areas.
The CPI(M) has also been in the field but is maintaining a low-key approach as part of its strategy.
The party is organising some public meetings but is mostly focusing on door-to-door campaigning and small meetings.

stories.headline: Opposition calls for CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s removal after report on Election Commissioners’ dissent
stories.title: Opposition calls for CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s removal after report on Election Commissioners’ dissent
stories.summary: Both ECs recorded formal objections regarding centralisation of poll roll database, “illegal” changes in Form 6, removal of voters in West Bengal, Goa; terming the CEC the “chief architect of vote chori”, Congress calls for SC-monitored probe
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Opposition parties on Wednesday (September 23, 2026) sought the removal of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar after an Indian Express expose claimed that two of the three Election Commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had formally recorded objections at least 14 times over the last 10 months.
The two ECs said major decisions were being made in the name of the full Election Commission of India without their knowledge, several of which they called “unauthorised and illegal”.

Declaring that “vote chori” is a crime against the Indian people and a direct attack on the Constitution, the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi said that “the BJP, RSS and EC who organised it have committed an act of treason.
Justice will be served.” He will hold a press conference on the matter on Thursday.

Opposition parties asked the Supreme Court to take suo motu cognisance of the report and Congress leader K.C. Venugopal demanded a Supreme Court-monitored impartial investigation to “expose the rot that has destroyed the ECI’s credibility”.
The CEC has no right to remain in office after the expose, he said.
The ECI responded on Wednesday (September 23, 2026), saying that all its actions have been in accordance with laws and instructions of the Commission.

Highlighting specific internal notes or observations spread over the 10-month period while overlooking the much larger body of approvals, decisions, instructions, and initiatives gives only “one part of the picture”, it said.
According to the Indian Express report, both Election Commissioners red-flagged several key issues, led by the centralisation of the database of electoral rolls.
In May, Mr. Joshi had reportedly proposed an audit to certify that “no one except the concerned statutory authorities has any credentials to make any change in the data base”.

In August, Mr. Sandhu had recorded that State-level election officials were reporting that they do not have “proper and complete access” to the ERONet portal, the digital system through which the electoral rolls are maintained.

He further flagged that the Commission’s director general of information technology Seema Khanna “does not have any legal authority to restrict proper and complete access and freedom to operate as given by law to the statutory authorities”.

stories.headline: Who appoints India’s Election Commissioners? Supreme Court sends law challenge to larger bench
stories.title: Who appoints India’s Election Commissioners? Supreme Court sends law challenge to larger bench
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court's latest move puts the 2023 law governing Election Commission appointments under fresh constitutional scrutiny as the ECI faces a separate row over SIR and electoral-roll decisions.

New Delhi: The Supreme Court has moved the challenge to the 2023 law governing the appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners towards a larger Constitution Bench, bringing the ECI’s appointment process into sharper focus at a time when the poll panel is facing a separate controversy over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday directed that petitions challenging the 2023 law governing the appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners be placed before the Chief Justice of India for constitution of a larger bench.
The development came after a two-judge bench comprising Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma differed over whether the challenge required consideration by a Constitution Bench.
The judges ultimately agreed that sending the matter through another preliminary reference could cause further delay.
The case concerns the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.
Under the law, the three-member selection committee consists of the Prime Minister, a Union Cabinet minister nominated by the Prime Minister and the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha.

The law replaced the arrangement laid down by the Supreme Court in its 2023 Anoop Baranwal judgment, under which the Prime Minister, Leader of Opposition and Chief Justice of India were to select the Election Commissioners until Parliament enacted legislation on the subject.
Justice Dipankar Datta questioned whether the present selection mechanism provides sufficient independence from the executive.
He observed that the Election Commission must not only be independent but must also appear independent.
Justice Satish Chandra Sharma took the view that the constitutional questions raised by the challenge should be considered authoritatively by a Constitution Bench.
The disagreement resulted in the matter being sent to the CJI for appropriate bench formation.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Refers Pleas Challenging Election Commissioners' Law To Constitution Bench; Justice Datta Questions Selection Process
stories.title: Supreme Court Refers Pleas Challenging Election Commissioners' Law To Constitution Bench; Justice Datta Questions Selection Process
stories.summary: Justice Datta prima facie doubted whether the present appointment process for Election Commissioners was independent.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence

article_sentences: Justice Datta prima facie doubted whether the present appointment process for Election Commissioners was independent.
The Supreme Court on Wednesday referred the petitions challenging the 2023 law governing the appointment process for the Chief Election Commissioners and Election Commissioners to a larger bench.

Even though a two-judge bench of Justice Dipankar Datta and Justice Satish Chandra Sharma disagreed on whether the matter should be referred, they ultimately ordered that the matter be placed before the CJI for the constitution of a Constitution Bench of appropriate strength, to avoid further delay.
The bench observed that referring the matter to a 3-judge bench on the preliminary point of reference would be a time-consuming exercise.
While Justice Datta opined the Union's demand for a larger bench reference was unwarranted, Justice Sharma held otherwise.
Justice Datta prima facie questioned whether the 2023 law governing the appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners provides an independent selection process.

Justice Datta observed that the 2023 Act, prima facie, appeared to confer a veto on the Executive, since the appointment process, by a committee comprising the PM, Union Minister and the Leader of Opposition, fails the "perception trust."
Justice Datta observed that a nominee of the Prime Minister cannot be expected to vote against the Prime Minister.
"Free and fair elections depend on a truly independent ECI.
It is not enough for the ECI to be independent; it must appear to be independent.
The member nominated by the Prime Minister cannot be expected to defy the Prime Minister," Justice Datta observed.

The Minister nominated by the Prime Minister to function as the third member of the selection committee, chaired by the Prime Minister, cannot be expected to defy his own nominator and risk his continuation as such nominated member on the committee for all practical purposes.

stories.headline: Are India's Wind Developers Being Priced Out Of The Market?
stories.title: Are India's Wind Developers Being Priced Out Of The Market?
stories.summary: Germany's Federal Network Agency, Bundesnetzagentur, closed its latest onshore wind auction this week with a number renewable planners everywhere should sit up for: 461 bids worth 5,250 MW chasing just 2,520 MW on offer, more than double the tendered capacity. It is the latest in a run of oversubscribed German wind rounds this year. Regulators awarded 237 projects totalling 2,523 MW at prices between 4.49 and 4.98 euro cents per kWh, pulling the weighted-average award price down to 4.79 cents, from 5.06 cents in the previous round. That is not an isolated data point. WindEurope's reading of the German pipeline points to the real driver behind it: permitting. Germany cleared roughly 21 GW of onshore wind permits last year and is on pace to beat that total in 2026, building a backlog of ready-to-build projects large enough that developers now compete hard on price rather than scramble to find viable sites. Lower Saxony alone picked up 836 MW of the latest round, followed by North Rhine-Westphalia and Rhineland-Palatinate. Same Price, Different Pipeline Contrast that with India's own wind story. The Solar Energy Corporation of India's (SECI) 2,000 MW ISTS-connected wind tender concluded in July 2026 with just 1,495 MW awarded , 505 MW short, at tariffs between Rs 3.78 and Rs 4.32 per kWh, roughly 4.5 to 5.2 US cents, a range that sits close to what German developers are now accepting. That is not a new pattern, as prioces have climbed up since 2022, when the last lows were discovered . SECI wind tenders have repeatedly struggled to find full subscription over the years, with developers and analysts pointing again and again to the same two culprits: a shrinking pool of premium sites with clear land titles, and delays in interstate transmission connectivity that leave even well-priced projects unbuildable within tender timelines. India's fundamentals are not the obstacle. The country holds an estimated wind potential of nearly 700 GW at 120 metres and has built domestic manufacturing capacity of 18 GW a year, yet installed wind capacity stood at barely 59 GW as of August 2026, a fraction of what the resource and the factories could support. The constraint sits upstream of the auction, in land acquisition, forest and transmission clearances, and the pace at which the Central Transmission Utility can string new evacuation corridors to wind-rich corners of Gujarat, Rajasthan, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu . The Permitting Advantage Germany's experience offers an unglamorous but replicable lesson: pre-clear the pipeline, and the auction takes care of price discovery on its own. Federal and state permitting authorities there spent the past two years working through a backlog under the EU's revised Renewable Energy Directive, which set binding timelines for permitting decisions. The result now shows up as auction oversubscription rather than auction failure, and prices keep falling as competition among ready projects intensifies. India has moved on pieces of this problem, including green energy corridor investments and recent efforts to fast-track ISTS connectivity for renewable clusters. But the wind segment, unlike solar, has not seen a comparable acceleration in ready-to-bid sites reaching tender stage. Until the project pipeline ahead of each auction is deep enough that developers are competing for scarce contracts rather than assembling land under deadline pressure, India's wind tenders are likely to keep landing short of target even as global capital and turbine capacity stand ready and waiting. A clear, formal policy on repowering has also eluded developers so far, that would open up a 20 GW market worth at least worth 5 years of new wind energy installations in one go. There is also a climate-finance dimension worth noting. Germany's falling award prices are feeding directly into cheaper long-term power purchase agreements for corporates and utilities, which in turn makes wind bankable to a wider pool of lenders. India's undersubscribed rounds have the opposite effect: lenders read a pattern of shortfalls as a signal of execution risk, which raises the cost of capital for the very projects that do get built, even when the underlying tariff looks competitive on paper. Breaking that cycle may matter as much for India's climate-finance ambitions as any single policy tweak to the auction design itself.

stories.title: Auto taxi unions move supreme court against Karnataka bike taxi ruling
stories.summary: Five Karnataka auto and taxi drivers’ organisations have moved the Supreme Court challenging the High Court ruling permitting bike taxis, citing regulatory parity, safety concerns and livelihood implications for existing operators.

article_sentences: Five Karnataka auto and taxi drivers’ organisations have moved the Supreme Court challenging the High Court ruling permitting bike taxis, citing regulatory parity, safety concerns and livelihood implications for existing operators.

Bengaluru: Five auto-rickshaw and taxi drivers’ organisations in Karnataka have approached the Supreme Court challenging the Karnataka High Court’s January 23 order that paved the way for bike taxis to operate as contract carriages in the state.

The petitioners include Nadaprabhu Kempegowda Auto Drivers’ Organisation, Karnataka Venkategowda Auto and Taxi Drivers’ Association, Greater Bengaluru Drivers’ Association, Karnataka Sarathigala Mahasangha and Jai Karnataka Sarathi Sena Trust.

The unions have questioned the High Court’s direction to the state government to consider applications seeking registration of motorcycles as transport vehicles and permits to operate them as contract carriages.
They have argued that decisions relating to transport policy and regulation fall within the domain of the government and statutory transport authorities.

According to the petition, the High Court’s order effectively creates a regulatory pathway for bike taxis and could have consequences for thousands of existing auto-rickshaw and taxi operators who are already functioning under a detailed regulatory framework.
The petitioners have highlighted the livelihood concerns of conventional transport operators in Bengaluru.

They have claimed that around 1.5 lakh auto drivers, taxi permit holders and other regulated transport operators could be affected if bike taxis are allowed to compete without being subjected to comparable regulatory requirements.
Existing auto-rickshaws and taxis are required to comply with conditions relating to permits, vehicle fitness, insurance, taxation, fare regulation and driver licensing.
The unions have argued that allowing another category of passenger transport without equivalent obligations could raise questions about regulatory parity and passenger safety.
The petition also refers to a 2019 expert committee report, which, according to the unions, had raised concerns about permitting bike taxis in Bengaluru.
Issues cited included road safety, traffic congestion, efficient use of road space and pollution.

The petitioners have highlighted the livelihood concerns of conventional transport operators in Bengaluru.

stories.headline: Arunachal Pradesh State Cabinet approves panel for survey of Siang mega dam
stories.title: Arunachal Pradesh State Cabinet approves panel for survey of Siang mega dam
stories.summary: Many villagers have been opposing the bid to prepare the pre-feasibility report for the proposed Siang Upper Multipurpose Project, which will generate an estimated 11,000 MW of electricity
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence

candidate gate: no category but HIGH+ priority -> allowed
article_sentences: Amid protests, the Arunachal Pradesh State Cabinet on Wednesday (September 23, 2026) adopted a resolution approving the constitution of an Empowered High-Level Committee “to guide and coordinate” the pre-feasibility report survey and associated activities for the proposed Siang Upper Multipurpose Project or SUMP.
Villagers along the Siang River belt are resisting the pre-feasibility report for the project, which will generate an estimated 11,000 megawatts (MW) or more of hydroelectricity.
Two of the project’s three designated sites are in Siang district, and one is in Upper Siang district.
The State Cabinet, headed by Chief Minister Pema Khandu, noted that the Union government had declared SUMP to be a national project in 2008, underlining its strategic significance for the country.

It also noted that the project could strengthen water and energy security, help mitigate floods in the Siang-Brahmaputra basin, generate employment, and support long-term socio-economic development of the Siang region.

“The resolution reflects the State government’s continuing commitment to ensuring that the survey is carried out in a transparent, peaceful, and people-centric manner,” a statement from the Chief Minister’s Office said.
The Cabinet underlined concerns raised by some sections of the people in Siang and Upper Siang districts “regarding misinformation and disinformation” being spread by certain vested interests.
It resolved that conducting the pre-feasibility report peacefully depended on sustained, meaningful engagement with the residents of these two districts.
“The voices, welfare, and aspirations of the likely project-affected families and local communities have always been, and will always remain, central to the process,” the State Cabinet said.
Meanwhile, local authorities organised a series of interactive school exhibitions on the SUMP, involving 640 students across four schools in Siang district.

“The exhibitions formed part of a targeted educational outreach initiative to foster awareness about river management, sustainable hydropower, and the SUMP among students in Rumgong, Kaying and Pessing villages that may be affected by the project,” an official statement said.
The Centre and State governments have defended the SUMP, insisting it was needed to counter the 60,000 MW project China is constructing on the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet.
